screens.title: Cache Eviction Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Caches store hot data to speed systems, but every cache has a fixed capacity. When it fills, we must remove an item to insert new data. That choice—the eviction policy—directly shapes hit rates and latency. In this chapter you'll learn the rules designers commonly use: Least Recently Used, Least Frequently Used, First-In First-Out, Most Recently Used, and the adaptive ARC approach. We'll see how each policy tracks usage, which workloads they favor, and where they fail. For example, LRU leverages temporal locality but is vulnerable to sequential scans. LFU captures long-term popularity but can keep stale items. FIFO is extremely simple but often inefficient. ARC tries to blend LRU and LFU to adapt to mixed patterns. Understanding these trade-offs helps you pick or design a cache that fits your workload and performance goals. By the end, you will be able to articulate when a policy will help or hurt, explain implementation costs like time and memory overhead, and run small simulations to compare behavior.

screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will explain why eviction is necessary in finite caches, describe the mechanisms behind common policies, analyze strengths and weaknesses for different access patterns, and identify practical scenarios favoring one policy over another. You will also understand ARC as a higher‑level adaptive strategy. Each objective is framed as a measurable competency: explain, describe, analyze, and identify. For example, you'll be able to say why LRU suits trending content on a news site, or why LFU resists pollution from single-pass scans. You'll also learn to evaluate implementation costs like maintaining frequency counters or linked lists and how those costs affect throughput and latency in high-performance caches. screens.title: Why eviction is required
screens.narratorSegment: A cache stores fast copies of data, but every cache has finite capacity. When capacity is reached and a new item must be inserted, eviction policies decide which existing item to remove. This is not just bookkeeping — eviction rules shape which data remains available and therefore drive the cache's hit rate. Consider a small Redis instance with limited memory: if it keeps rarely used keys, frequently requested items will miss and the application will suffer latency spikes. A clear definition: cache eviction is the process of removing items from a full cache to make space for new entries, while an eviction policy is the algorithm determining which items to remove. A concrete example helps: imagine a web cache holding 100 pages where a sudden analytics job reads 10,000 unique pages once. Without the right policy, this scan can evict valuable pages, producing a dramatic drop in hit rate. A common misconception is that a more complex policy always wins; in fact, complexity costs C P U and memory and can reduce throughput under heavy load. The right approach balances predictiveness of the rule with its implementation cost. Reflect: what access pattern most affects your service — repeated reads or wide scans? That question guides policy choice.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Eviction is necessary to free space in finite caches; the chosen policy determines which items are kept and which are removed, affecting hit rate and performance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Why eviction is required
Finite caches need eviction rules
A precise definition and a real-world consequence.
Formal definition

Cache eviction removes items when capacity is exceeded. The eviction policy is the rule selecting the victim.

Why it matters
  • Controls hit rate and latency.
  • Affects throughput due to tracking overhead.
  • Mistakes cause cache pollution and poor performance.
Concrete example

A 100-item page cache is flushed by a one-time analytics scan of 10,000 unique pages; if eviction favors recent inserts, important pages can be evicted and subsequent user requests miss.

Key Takeaway

Eviction policy must match workload patterns; otherwise the cache can harm performance more than it helps.

Common misconceptions
  • "More complex policy is always better" — complexity can add CPU and memory overhead and reduce throughput.
  • "One policy fits all workloads" — different access patterns require different strategies.
Real-world connection

Service designers must measure access patterns before choosing a policy. Testing with real traces or simulations often reveals surprising behaviors.

screens.title: Least Recently Used (LRU)
screens.narratorSegment: Least Recently Used uses the idea of temporal locality: recently accessed items are likely to be accessed again soon. LRU therefore evicts the item that hasn't been used for the longest period. A typical efficient implementation uses a hash map for O(1) lookups and a doubly linked list to maintain access order; when an item is accessed it's moved to the most-recent end, and eviction removes the least-recent end. The Python example in this chapter uses OrderedDict to achieve that behavior. A concrete example: with capacity two, inserting keys 1 and 2 then accessing 1 makes 2 the least recently used; inserting key 3 evicts 2. A common misconception is that LRU always handles scans well — it does not. Sequentially reading a large number of unique items will push out useful cached entries because each new item becomes the most recent and older but still useful items get evicted. Implementation costs include maintaining the list and map, and occasional pointer adjustments; in high throughput caches, that overhead can matter. When you expect strong temporal locality, LRU is an excellent default; otherwise test with traces.

keyIdea.text: LRU keeps recently used items and evicts the item unused for the longest time; efficient implementations combine a hash map and a doubly linked list.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Least Recently Used (LRU)
Least Recently Used
Evict the least recently accessed item; common default for temporal locality.
Code example (Python)
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
  def __init__(self, capacity):
    self.capacity = capacity
    self.cache = OrderedDict()

  def get(self, key):
    if key not in self.cache:
      return -1
    value = self.cache.pop(key)
    self.cache[key] = value
    return value

  def put(self, key, value):
    if key in self.cache:
      self.cache.pop(key)
    elif len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:
      self.cache.popitem(last=False)
    self.cache[key] = value
OrderedDict moves accessed items to the end, so the front is the LRU item.
Example scenario

Capacity 2: put(1), put(2), get(1) makes 2 LRU; put(3) evicts 2. LRU retained the recently used key 1.

Trade-offs
  • Pros: aligns with temporal locality, simple concept.
  • Cons: vulnerable to scan patterns; tracking overhead.
Key Takeaway

LRU is a strong default when recent access predicts future use, but verify with workload traces.

screens.title: Least Frequently Used (LFU)
screens.narratorSegment: Least Frequently Used tracks how often items are accessed and evicts the item with the smallest access count. The central claim is that items with higher cumulative frequency are more valuable. Practically, each cache entry maintains a frequency counter that increments on access; on eviction the lowest-count entry is removed, and ties are typically broken by recency. A concrete example: if item A is accessed 100 times over an hour and item B only once, LFU will prioritize A even if B was recently accessed. This makes LFU robust against short-lived scans: a single access in a large scan won't immediately protect that scanned item. But LFU has its own pitfall — it can retain once-popular items that are no longer relevant, causing stale data to occupy space. Implementations often add aging or decay to mitigate this. Another misconception is that LFU needs very heavy bookkeeping; while it is more complex than LRU, practical variants keep per-key counters and use buckets or min-heaps to organize items. Consider LFU when you expect stable, long-term popularity rather than fleeting bursts. Least Frequently Used (LFU) means lfu evicts the least frequently accessed item, favoring long-term popularity but requiring frequency tracking and mechanisms to handle stale counts.. In practical terms, using frequency to prefer long-term popularity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Least Frequently Used (LFU)
Least Frequently Used
Evict the item with the lowest access count; good for long-term popularity.
How it works
  • Each item has a frequency counter incremented on access.
  • Evict the item with the lowest count; break ties by recency.
Concrete example

If A has count 100 and B has count 1, LFU keeps A even if B was accessed more recently.

Pros & Cons
  • Pros: Resists single-pass scan pollution; retains enduringly popular items.
  • Cons: Can keep stale popular items; more bookkeeping required.
Mitigations for staleness

Use decaying counters, periodic aging, or sliding-window frequency to reduce retention of once-popular items.

Key Takeaway

LFU excels when popularity is stable over time, but add aging to avoid keeping stale data forever.

screens.title: FIFO and MRU
screens.narratorSegment: First-In First-Out is the simplest eviction policy: evict the oldest item by insertion time. FIFO treats the cache like a queue where new items join the back and the front is removed when capacity is full. It is easy to implement and low overhead, but it ignores both recency and frequency, so it tends to have low hit rates for typical workloads. A concrete example: if your cache contains popular items that were inserted earlier, FIFO can evict them simply because they are old, even if they are frequently accessed. Most Recently Used, by contrast, evicts the item accessed most recently. MRU seems counterintuitive, but it can be effective in niche cases where items are consumed once then not reused — for example, when iterating through unique stream elements in an ETL job. A common misconception is to assume FIFO is acceptable because "it is simple"; for most performance-critical caches it's too naive. Another is to assume MRU is always bad; instead, recognize specialized workloads where evicting the most recent item prevents retention of one-time accesses. Use FIFO only for very low-overhead, non-performance-critical caches, and consider MRU only for rare single-use streams.

keyIdea.text: FIFO is simple but often poor in hit-rate; MRU is niche but useful when recent items are unlikely to be reused.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › FIFO & MRU
FIFO and MRU
Compare the simplest and the counterintuitive policies.
FIFO (First-In, First-Out)

Evict by insertion order. Implement with a queue for minimal overhead.

When it fails

Commonly evicts useful items and yields low hit rate for workloads with temporal locality.

MRU (Most Recently Used)

Evict the item that was accessed most recently. Useful when recent items are unlikely to be reused.

Niche use

Useful for single-pass streams where once-used data won't be needed again.

Example comparison
FIFO scenario
Simple queue; cheap updates; poor hit rate when access patterns favor recent items.
MRU scenario
Use when items are consumed once; prevents one-time items from blocking older cache entries.

screens.title: Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC)
screens.narratorSegment: ARC combines the strengths of LRU and LFU by maintaining two LRU lists: one for recently accessed items and one for frequently accessed items, and it adapts the sizes of those lists based on observed hits. The claim is that adaptive balancing often outperforms either pure LRU or LFU across mixed workloads. Concretely, ARC keeps a list for recent items and a list for frequent items, plus two 'ghost' lists that remember recent evictions. By monitoring whether recent hits come from the recent or frequent list, ARC adjusts how much space is allocated to each. An example: during a scan-heavy phase, ARC can give more space to the frequent list to avoid pollution; when temporal locality appears, it shifts to favor recent items. The trade-off is complexity: ARC requires multiple lists, ghost entries, and dynamic bookkeeping, increasing C P U and memory overhead. A common misconception is that ARC is magically superior; it is robust across mixed patterns but not always worth the extra operational cost. Use ARC when you face varied workloads and can afford the implementation overhead. Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) means arc dynamically balances recent and frequent lru lists using ghost entries to adapt to changing workloads and resist scan pollution.. In practical terms, blending recency and frequency with dynamic adaptation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC)
Adaptive Replacement Cache
An adaptive policy that balances recency and frequency to handle mixed workloads.
Key components
  • Two LRU lists: recent and frequent.
  • Two ghost lists remembering recent evictions for adaptation.
  • Dynamic adjustment of list sizes based on hit rates.
Behavior example

If hits start coming more from the frequent list, ARC increases its size; if recent accesses dominate, it shifts capacity to recent items.

Pros & Cons
  • Pros: robust across mixed patterns, resists scan pollution.
  • Cons: higher implementation complexity and CPU/memory overhead.
Key Takeaway

ARC adapts between recent and frequent lists to be broadly effective, but only choose it when its overhead is justified.

screens.title: Implementation costs and complexity
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing an eviction policy requires balancing predictive benefit against implementation cost. For each policy, consider get and put time complexity and memory overhead for bookkeeping. LRU typically achieves O(1) for get and put using a hash map plus a doubly linked list, but pointer operations add C P U work and memory per entry for list nodes. LFU requires frequency counters; naive implementations may need min-heaps or ordered buckets, increasing complexity and memory. FIFO uses a simple queue and is very cheap, but that low cost comes with poor hit-rate for common workloads. ARC demands multiple lists and ghost entries, which raises both C P U and memory costs. A concrete example: in a high-throughput Redis instance, an O(1) LRU might still be chosen over LFU because the additional counter updates in LFU or multi-list adjustments in ARC could add measurable latency under peak traffic. A common misconception is to ignore operational constraints—if your cache is already C P U-bound, adding complex eviction logic can worsen latency. Always test: measure latency and throughput trade-offs when switching policies, and consider simplified variants like sampled LFU or LRU-K to lower overhead while addressing specific weaknesses.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Implementation Costs
Time and memory trade-offs
Evaluate complexity before adopting advanced policies.
LRU
O(1) ops with map + linked list; moderate per-entry memory.
LFU
Counters and buckets or heaps; higher bookkeeping cost.
ARC
Multiple lists and ghost entries; best for mixed workloads but costly.
Practical guidance
  • Profile the cache under realistic load before changing policy.
  • Prefer simpler policies if CPU is the bottleneck.
  • Consider hybrid or sampled approaches to reduce overhead.

screens.title: Cache pollution and scan resistance
screens.narratorSegment: Cache pollution occurs when a workload inserts items that are unlikely to be reused and thereby evicts useful data. A common source is a large sequential scan or batch job that touches many unique keys. LRU is especially vulnerable: a scan will mark newly inserted items as most recent, pushing previously useful entries out. LFU resists this, because a single access only increments frequency by one. Concrete defensive techniques include: using LFU or ARC which resist scan pollution, adding admission filters that deny caching of single-touch items, or using a separate cold queue for new entries (2Q or LRU-K variants). Another approach is to detect scan-like behavior and throttle caching during that window. A misconception is to treat scans as normal traffic; they often require special handling. Ask: can you identify a batch process in your system that might be accidentally poisoning your cache? If so, consider a short-lived bypass or an admission policy to prevent pollution while preserving cache value for real user traffic. Cache pollution and scan resistance means detect scans and use admission policies, lfu, arc, or two-queue variants to prevent one-time accesses from evicting valuable items.. In practical terms, how scans and batch jobs harm caches and how to defend. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Another approach is to detect scan-like behavior and throttle caching during that window. A misconception is to treat scans as normal traffic; they often require special handling. Ask: can you identify a batch process in your system that might be accidentally poisoning your cache? If so, consider a short-lived bypass or an admission policy to prevent pollution while preserving cache value for real user traffic. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Hands-on: FIFO vs LRU
Compare FIFO and LRU
Implementations and a simple simulation illustrate differences.
FIFOCache example
from collections import deque

class FIFOCache:
  def __init__(self, capacity):
    self.capacity = capacity
    self.cache = {}
    self.queue = deque()

  def get(self, key):
    return self.cache.get(key)

  def put(self, key, value):
    if key in self.cache:
      self.cache[key] = value
    else:
      if len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:
        evicted = self.queue.popleft()
        del self.cache[evicted]
      self.cache[key] = value
      self.queue.append(key)
LRUCache reminder
from collections import OrderedDict

class LRUCache:
  def __init__(self, capacity):
    self.capacity = capacity
    self.cache = OrderedDict()

  def get(self, key):
    if key not in self.cache:
      return -1
    val = self.cache.pop(key)
    self.cache[key] = val
    return val

  def put(self, key, value):
    if key in self.cache:
      self.cache.pop(key)
    elif len(self.cache) >= self.capacity:
      self.cache.popitem(last=False)
    self.cache[key] = value
Simulation hints
  • Run identical sequences on both caches and log evictions.
  • Count hits and misses and compare totals.
  • Check edge cases: updates to existing keys, and behavior under sequential scans.

screens.title: Choosing an eviction policy
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting a policy begins with characterizing your workload. Ask these questions: are accesses bursty and recent, are there stable hot items, or do you face large scans and batch jobs? If temporal locality dominates, LRU is a strong default. If long-term popularity matters and access patterns are stable, LFU may serve better. If you have mixed patterns or can't predict changes, ARC provides adaptive resilience at a higher cost. Use FIFO only when simplicity and minimal overhead trump hit rate. A concrete decision example: a news website with quickly trending articles benefits from LRU because reads are concentrated over short windows; a video platform with consistently popular titles over months might favor LFU. Also factor operational constraints: limited C P U argues for simpler policies. A useful misconception to avoid is optimizing purely for theoretical hit rate without testing raw latency under load. Always run simulations or A/B tests with real traces and measure latency, throughput, and C P U usage before production rollout. Final reflective question: which metric — hit rate, latency, or C P U cost — matters most to your service, and does your chosen policy improve that metric under real load?

screens.title: Assessing policy choices with tests
screens.narratorSegment: Testing eviction policies should combine simulation with real-world experiments. Start with a simulation that replays historical traces and computes hit/miss counts for each policy. The hands-on activity in this chapter shows how to log evictions and hits for FIFO and LRU. After simulation, perform controlled A/B tests in production or staging where a portion of requests use the new policy and you measure end-to-end latency, error rates, and C P U consumption. Concrete example: split 5% of reads to a candidate cache configuration and compare user-facing latency and cache hit rate over several hours, accounting for diurnal patterns. Watch for anomalies such as increased C P U utilization or cache thrashing during batch jobs. A common misconception is assuming improved hit rate always yields better user latency; bookkeeping costs can offset hit-rate gains. Finally, iterate: if a policy under test shows marginal hit-rate improvements but much higher C P U, consider simpler variants or admission controls. Your final evaluation should weigh both performance and operational cost. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's wrap up the essential terms to remember. First, cache eviction is the removal of items from a full cache to make room for new data. Second, an eviction policy is the algorithm deciding which items to evict; common choices are LRU, LFU, FIFO, MRU, and ARC. Third, LRU evicts the item least recently used and works well when recent access predicts future access. Fourth, LFU evicts the least frequently used item and favors long-term popularity but risks keeping stale data. Fifth, FIFO evicts by insertion order and is simple but often inefficient. Sixth, MRU evicts the most recently used item and is useful only in special single-use scenarios. Finally, ARC adapts between recent and frequent lists and resists scan pollution at the cost of complexity. Keep these concise definitions in mind when analyzing caches and designing a caching layer for your system.

fullNarratorScript:
Caches store hot data to speed systems, but every cache has a fixed capacity. When it fills, we must remove an item to insert new data. That choice—the eviction policy—directly shapes hit rates and latency. In this chapter you'll learn the rules designers commonly use: Least Recently Used, Least Frequently Used, First-In First-Out, Most Recently Used, and the adaptive ARC approach. We'll see how each policy tracks usage, which workloads they favor, and where they fail. For example, LRU leverages temporal locality but is vulnerable to sequential scans. LFU captures long-term popularity but can keep stale items. FIFO is extremely simple but often inefficient. ARC tries to blend LRU and LFU to adapt to mixed patterns. Understanding these trade-offs helps you pick or design a cache that fits your workload and performance goals. By the end, you will be able to articulate when a policy will help or hurt, explain implementation costs like time and memory overhead, and run small simulations to compare behavior.

By the end of this chapter you will explain why eviction is necessary in finite caches, describe the mechanisms behind common policies, analyze strengths and weaknesses for different access patterns, and identify practical scenarios favoring one policy over another. You will also understand ARC as a higher‑level adaptive strategy. Each objective is framed as a measurable competency: explain, describe, analyze, and identify. For example, you'll be able to say why LRU suits trending content on a news site, or why LFU resists pollution from single-pass scans. You'll also learn to evaluate implementation costs like maintaining frequency counters or linked lists and how those costs affect throughput and latency in high-performance caches. Finally, you'll practice by implementing FIFO and LRU in Python and running a small simulation to compare eviction behavior and hit rates. These skills matter because eviction decisions can turn a fast cache into a noisy, ineffective layer if you choose incorrectly. Think of objectives as checkpoints: after each one you should be able to justify a policy choice using workload characteristics and data structures rather than guesswork.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical evaluation and testing. You will implement and simulate FIFO and LRU in Python, run a sequence of puts and gets, and interpret eviction logs to compute hit and miss counts. The hands-on activity in this chapter walks you through a small experiment that contrasts how FIFO and LRU behave on the same sequence of accesses. You will learn to set up simple measurements: count hits, count evictions, and reason about why one policy produced more misses. Additionally, you will assess implementation overhead: time complexity for get and put operations and memory used for structures like counters or linked lists. Finally, you'll practice recognizing workload signals — for instance, a one‑time large scan or short-lived trending items — and map them to a policy choice, including when ARC might be worth the extra complexity. These objectives help you move from conceptual knowledge to practical evaluation and clear decision-making.

A cache stores fast copies of data, but every cache has finite capacity. When capacity is reached and a new item must be inserted, eviction policies decide which existing item to remove. This is not just bookkeeping — eviction rules shape which data remains available and therefore drive the cache's hit rate. Consider a small Redis instance with limited memory: if it keeps rarely used keys, frequently requested items will miss and the application will suffer latency spikes. A clear definition: cache eviction is the process of removing items from a full cache to make space for new entries, while an eviction policy is the algorithm determining which items to remove. A concrete example helps: imagine a web cache holding 100 pages where a sudden analytics job reads 10,000 unique pages once. Without the right policy, this scan can evict valuable pages, producing a dramatic drop in hit rate. A common misconception is that a more complex policy always wins; in fact, complexity costs C P U and memory and can reduce throughput under heavy load. The right approach balances predictiveness of the rule with its implementation cost. Reflect: what access pattern most affects your service — repeated reads or wide scans? That question guides policy choice.

Least Recently Used uses the idea of temporal locality: recently accessed items are likely to be accessed again soon. LRU therefore evicts the item that hasn't been used for the longest period. A typical efficient implementation uses a hash map for O(1) lookups and a doubly linked list to maintain access order; when an item is accessed it's moved to the most-recent end, and eviction removes the least-recent end. The Python example in this chapter uses OrderedDict to achieve that behavior. A concrete example: with capacity two, inserting keys 1 and 2 then accessing 1 makes 2 the least recently used; inserting key 3 evicts 2. A common misconception is that LRU always handles scans well — it does not. Sequentially reading a large number of unique items will push out useful cached entries because each new item becomes the most recent and older but still useful items get evicted. Implementation costs include maintaining the list and map, and occasional pointer adjustments; in high throughput caches, that overhead can matter. When you expect strong temporal locality, LRU is an excellent default; otherwise test with traces.

Least Frequently Used tracks how often items are accessed and evicts the item with the smallest access count. The central claim is that items with higher cumulative frequency are more valuable. Practically, each cache entry maintains a frequency counter that increments on access; on eviction the lowest-count entry is removed, and ties are typically broken by recency. A concrete example: if item A is accessed 100 times over an hour and item B only once, LFU will prioritize A even if B was recently accessed. This makes LFU robust against short-lived scans: a single access in a large scan won't immediately protect that scanned item. But LFU has its own pitfall — it can retain once-popular items that are no longer relevant, causing stale data to occupy space. Implementations often add aging or decay to mitigate this. Another misconception is that LFU needs very heavy bookkeeping; while it is more complex than LRU, practical variants keep per-key counters and use buckets or min-heaps to organize items. Consider LFU when you expect stable, long-term popularity rather than fleeting bursts. Least Frequently Used (LFU) means lfu evicts the least frequently accessed item, favoring long-term popularity but requiring frequency tracking and mechanisms to handle stale counts.. In practical terms, using frequency to prefer long-term popularity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

First-In First-Out is the simplest eviction policy: evict the oldest item by insertion time. FIFO treats the cache like a queue where new items join the back and the front is removed when capacity is full. It is easy to implement and low overhead, but it ignores both recency and frequency, so it tends to have low hit rates for typical workloads. A concrete example: if your cache contains popular items that were inserted earlier, FIFO can evict them simply because they are old, even if they are frequently accessed. Most Recently Used, by contrast, evicts the item accessed most recently. MRU seems counterintuitive, but it can be effective in niche cases where items are consumed once then not reused — for example, when iterating through unique stream elements in an ETL job. A common misconception is to assume FIFO is acceptable because "it is simple"; for most performance-critical caches it's too naive. Another is to assume MRU is always bad; instead, recognize specialized workloads where evicting the most recent item prevents retention of one-time accesses. Use FIFO only for very low-overhead, non-performance-critical caches, and consider MRU only for rare single-use streams.

ARC combines the strengths of LRU and LFU by maintaining two LRU lists: one for recently accessed items and one for frequently accessed items, and it adapts the sizes of those lists based on observed hits. The claim is that adaptive balancing often outperforms either pure LRU or LFU across mixed workloads. Concretely, ARC keeps a list for recent items and a list for frequent items, plus two 'ghost' lists that remember recent evictions. By monitoring whether recent hits come from the recent or frequent list, ARC adjusts how much space is allocated to each. An example: during a scan-heavy phase, ARC can give more space to the frequent list to avoid pollution; when temporal locality appears, it shifts to favor recent items. The trade-off is complexity: ARC requires multiple lists, ghost entries, and dynamic bookkeeping, increasing C P U and memory overhead. A common misconception is that ARC is magically superior; it is robust across mixed patterns but not always worth the extra operational cost. Use ARC when you face varied workloads and can afford the implementation overhead. Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) means arc dynamically balances recent and frequent lru lists using ghost entries to adapt to changing workloads and resist scan pollution.. In practical terms, blending recency and frequency with dynamic adaptation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing an eviction policy requires balancing predictive benefit against implementation cost. For each policy, consider get and put time complexity and memory overhead for bookkeeping. LRU typically achieves O(1) for get and put using a hash map plus a doubly linked list, but pointer operations add C P U work and memory per entry for list nodes. LFU requires frequency counters; naive implementations may need min-heaps or ordered buckets, increasing complexity and memory. FIFO uses a simple queue and is very cheap, but that low cost comes with poor hit-rate for common workloads. ARC demands multiple lists and ghost entries, which raises both C P U and memory costs. A concrete example: in a high-throughput Redis instance, an O(1) LRU might still be chosen over LFU because the additional counter updates in LFU or multi-list adjustments in ARC could add measurable latency under peak traffic. A common misconception is to ignore operational constraints—if your cache is already C P U-bound, adding complex eviction logic can worsen latency. Always test: measure latency and throughput trade-offs when switching policies, and consider simplified variants like sampled LFU or LRU-K to lower overhead while addressing specific weaknesses.

Cache pollution occurs when a workload inserts items that are unlikely to be reused and thereby evicts useful data. A common source is a large sequential scan or batch job that touches many unique keys. Let's wrap up the essential terms to remember. First, cache eviction is the removal of items from a full cache to make room for new data. Second, an eviction policy is the algorithm deciding which items to evict; common choices are LRU, LFU, FIFO, MRU, and ARC. Third, LRU evicts the item least recently used and works well when recent access predicts future access. Fourth, LFU evicts the least frequently used item and favors long-term popularity but risks keeping stale data. Fifth, FIFO evicts by insertion order and is simple but often inefficient. Sixth, MRU evicts the most recently used item and is useful only in special single-use scenarios. Finally, ARC adapts between recent and frequent lists and resists scan pollution at the cost of complexity. Keep these concise definitions in mind when analyzing caches and designing a caching layer for your system.

Three quick reminders to carry forward: first, the eviction policy you choose determines whether recent or frequent items persist, and that choice must reflect your workload. Second, watch out for cache pollution: scans and batch jobs can flush valuable entries unless the policy or admission logic prevents it. Third, complexity has cost: ARC and LFU provide robustness but require more bookkeeping; always validate whether their hit-rate improvements outweigh C P U and memory overhead. These three checks — workload match, pollution defense, and operational cost — form a practical triage you can apply when designing or tuning a cache.
